name: Moral Relativism
statement: Right and wrong are not absolute but relative to a culture, society, or individual's standpoint.
statementAccent: not absolute but relative to a culture, society, or individual's standpoint
meaning: Moral relativism is the view that moral judgments and truths are not absolute or universal but are relative to, and valid only within, some particular standpoint, such as a culture, society, historical period, or individual. On this view there are no objective, universal moral facts, and what is right or wrong depends on the norms of the group or person making the judgment, with no single standpoint uniquely privileged over all others. Moral relativism comes in distinct forms that should not be confused. Descriptive moral relativism is the empirical, anthropological observation that different cultures do in fact hold deeply different moral beliefs and practices; it is a factual claim, not itself a moral thesis, and is associated with anthropologists such as William Graham Sumner and Ruth Benedict. Metaethical moral relativism is the philosophical claim that the truth or justification of moral judgments is not absolute but relative to some group or standpoint, with no objective standard for adjudicating between them. Normative moral relativism is the more contested prescriptive claim, often about tolerance, that we ought to accept or refrain from judging the moral practices of others. Moral relativism contrasts with moral universalism, absolutism, and realism, which affirm objective universal moral truths, and it is a central and much-debated position in metaethics.
mechanism: Moral relativism denies that moral judgments have a single, objective standard of truth, holding instead that their truth or justification is indexed to a particular standpoint. The starting point for many relativists is descriptive: the empirical fact that human societies have held, and continue to hold, deeply divergent moral beliefs and practices, so that what one culture condemns another may celebrate. From this observation, metaethical relativism draws the further, philosophical conclusion that there is no framework-independent fact of the matter about who is right, so that a moral judgment is true or justified only relative to the norms of the culture or individual that makes it, and moral disagreement between frameworks cannot be rationally resolved by appeal to objective moral facts, because there are none. Different versions index moral truth to different standpoints: cultural relativism to the norms of a society, subjectivism to the attitudes of the individual. Some relativists add a normative claim, typically that because no morality is objectively privileged, one ought to tolerate the practices of other cultures and refrain from judging them, though this move is separable from and not entailed by the metaethical thesis. The mechanism throughout is the relativization of moral truth to a standpoint, in place of a universal standard.

examples.text: The factual observation that different cultures hold deeply different moral beliefs, a claim of anthropology, not itself a moral thesis.
The philosophical claim that moral truth is relative to a culture or individual, with no objective standard to adjudicate.
The contested normative claim that we ought to tolerate and not judge the moral practices of other cultures.

variants.name: Descriptive versus metaethical
variants.text: The factual observation of moral diversity versus the philosophical claim that moral truth is relative to a standpoint.

variants.name: Cultural versus individual
variants.text: Relativizing moral truth to the norms of a society, or to the attitudes of the individual, as in subjectivism.

whyItMatters: Moral relativism is a central and perennial position in metaethics, and the debate over it bears on the deepest questions about the status of morality. Its appeal is real and important: it is grounded in the undeniable fact of deep moral diversity across cultures, it counsels humility and tolerance in the face of that diversity, and it resists the arrogance of imposing one culture's values on others, a stance with significant appeal in an age of pluralism and after the abuses of imperialism. Engaging with moral relativism forces clarity about whether moral judgments can be objectively true, whether moral disagreement is genuine or merely apparent, and whether cross-cultural moral criticism can ever be justified. The position also serves as a foil that sharpens rival views, since defending moral realism or universalism requires answering the relativist's challenge from disagreement. Its practical stakes are high, touching debates about human rights, cultural practices, and the limits of tolerance.

working.text: note the empirical fact that cultures and individuals hold deeply different moral beliefs, descriptive relativism.
conclude, in metaethical relativism, that moral truth is relative to a standpoint with no objective standard between them.
some relativists further hold, normatively, that one ought to tolerate and not judge the practices of other frameworks.

limits: Moral relativism faces serious objections. The reformer's dilemma holds that if moral judgments are valid only relative to prevailing societal norms, then an internal moral reformer who criticizes those norms is wrong by definition, which seems to make moral reform and progress incoherent. Relativism also appears unable to condemn practices like slavery, genocide, or the atrocities of the Nazi regime as objectively wrong, since on its view they were right relative to the norms of the societies that practiced them, a conclusion many find unacceptable. A key logical objection is that the move from descriptive moral disagreement to metaethical relativism is a non-sequitur: the fact that people disagree does not by itself prove there is no objective fact, and skepticism or error could explain the disagreement equally well, while much apparent moral difference traces to differing factual beliefs over shared underlying values. The tolerance version is often charged with being self-refuting, since it states tolerance as a universal value.
misreadings: Moral relativism's descriptive form, that cultures differ morally, is a factual claim and does not by itself establish the philosophical claim that moral truth is relative, which is a separate and contested step. Relativism does not follow simply from moral disagreement, since disagreement is also explained by error or by differing factual beliefs over shared values. And the tolerance version is not entailed by metaethical relativism and is arguably self-refuting, so treating moral diversity as proving relativism, disagreement as settling the matter, or tolerance as a relativist conclusion, misreads a contested metaethical position.
origin: The metaethical view that moral judgments are relative to a culture, society, or individual rather than objective and universal, distinguished into descriptive, metaethical, and normative forms; a central and debated position in ethics.
